notes: Limited appeal on counterclaim expenditure; judge's wrong-version error and remission scope are clear.

enrichment.short_title: One Picture v Craig: remission of omitted counterclaim expenditure
key_facts: One Picture Ltd sued Timothy Craig to establish its copyright and trade mark rights in Hypermatter software; the judge rejected Craig's partnership claim and found he was a broker entitled to commission.

Craig's amended counterclaim included a paragraph 16(c) claim for recovery of expenditure incurred on behalf of the business, which the judge did not expressly address because he relied on the unamended counterclaim.
The judge awarded Craig £33,500 loan repayments and £5,440 expenses but refused interest and dismissed other counterclaim relief.
On limited permission to appeal on counterclaim points, the parties agreed the judge had failed to deal with paragraph 16(c).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with limited permission against Chancery Division judgment on counterclaim monetary relief.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: paragraph 16(c) remitted to the trial judge; interest ordered from 14 October 2002 on sums recovered; appellant's costs of the appeal awarded.
enrichment.ratio: Where a judge decides a counterclaim on the wrong version of the pleadings and fails expressly to determine a pleaded item of relief, that item should be remitted for determination; interest may run from the date of the original counterclaim even without a prior demand where the counterclaim put the other party on notice of the claim.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in failing to determine paragraph 16(c) of the amended counterclaim
Whether paragraph 17 damages inquiry should also be remitted
Whether interest should have been awarded on counterclaim sums
Whether the appeal on copyright issues fell within granted permission

confidence.notes: Limited appeal scope, remission order, and interest ruling are explicit. IP merits were not re-decided on appeal.

notes: Procedural judgment on whether an academic homelessness JR should continue; discrimination merits deferred.

enrichment.short_title: Morris v Westminster: whether academic homelessness JR should proceed
key_facts: A Mauritian mother with a dependent daughter challenged Westminster's refusal to treat her as in priority need because the child was subject to immigration control.
Keith J had held in October 2003 that section 185(4) required the council to disregard the child when assessing the mother's priority need.
Before the second hearing the daughter was registered as a British citizen in June 2003, but neither claimant's solicitors nor the court were informed until November 2003.
By May 2004 the claimant had employment, savings for private rent, and no wish for public housing; the Secretary of State intervened on Art 14/8 issues.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second judgment in judicial review deciding whether proceedings should continue after facts became academic.
enrichment.outcome: Claim permitted to proceed to a further hearing on discrimination, construction, and declaration issues despite the claimant no longer seeking accommodation.
enrichment.ratio: A judicial review claim may continue where the claimant no longer needs personal relief if appropriate declaratory relief remains available and the case is a suitable vehicle for resolving important legal issues on the facts as they stood when the decision was taken; Quintavelle governs the two-stage test of available relief and suitability.
legal_issues: Whether proceedings should continue when the claimant's circumstances had changed
Whether declaratory relief on section 185(4) and Art 14 ECHR remained appropriate
Whether the case was fact-sensitive to the point of being an unsuitable test case
Whether the claimant remained a victim under the HRA
linked_authorities: R v British Broadcasting Corporation ex p Quintavelle (1998) 10 Admin LR 425

confidence.notes: Procedural ruling to continue the claim is clear. Substantive discrimination and HRA issues were not decided in this judgment.

notes: Attorney General unduly lenient sentence reference; aggravating features and misleading mitigation are well documented.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference: six-month sentence increased for indecent assault on boy

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: Michael John Webb pleaded guilty to indecent assault on a 14-year-old boy who stayed overnight at his home before a football match.
Webb abused his position of trust, exploited the boy's family difficulties, and committed a prolonged assault including masturbation and anal penetration.
Judge Hall sentenced him to six months' imprisonment with an extended licence of two and a half years, heavily influenced by mitigation about Webb's teenage son having no alternative home.
The boy made a 999 call, developed PTSD, and the sentencing judge had been misled about the availability of accommodation with the offender's ex-partner.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference for leave to refer an indecent assault sentence as unduly lenient.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted; sentence increased to two years' imprisonment with a two-year extended licence; disqualification from working with children ordered.
enrichment.ratio: For serious indecent assault on a vulnerable child by a trusted adult, a sentence of about two and a half to three years was appropriate; undue weight had been given to the offender's personal circumstances and insufficient weight to harm, culpability, and deterrence; double jeopardy justified a two-year replacement sentence.
legal_issues: Whether six months' imprisonment was unduly lenient
Weight to be given to victim harm versus offender mitigation
Effect of misleading mitigation on the original sentence
Appropriate extended licence and ancillary orders

Attorney-General's Reference No 5 of 2001 (Terence Culshaw) [2001] 2 Cr App R (S) 473
Attorney-General's Reference No 41 of 2000 (David Harrison) [2001] 1 Cr App R (S) 372

confidence.notes: Agreed facts, sentencing outcome, and appellate reasoning are explicit throughout the judgment.

notes: Permission to appeal against EAT remission in unfair dismissal contributory conduct review; finality point arguable.

enrichment.short_title: Walker v Barnes: permission to appeal EAT remission on contributory conduct
key_facts: Mr Barnes succeeded in an unfair dismissal claim against Mr and Mrs Walker but his compensatory award was reduced by 30% for contributory conduct.
The employers had not paid the award and repeatedly sought review of the tribunal decision.
The EAT held the chairman had been perverse in refusing review of new evidence about a Cavanagh Construction arrangement potentially affecting the contribution deduction.
The EAT ordered remission for rehearing of the contributory conduct percentage before a differently constituted tribunal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision ordering remission.
enrichment.ratio: It is at least arguable that a tribunal chairman was better placed than the EAT to assess whether late-disclosed evidence could materially affect a contributory conduct deduction, and that remission to a fresh tribunal risks reopening the entire award contrary to the need for finality in employment litigation.
legal_issues: Whether the EAT was wrong to find the chairman's refusal of review perverse
Whether remission should be limited to the contribution percentage or risk reopening the whole award
Whether the new Cavanagh evidence passed the review tests
Whether permission to appeal should be granted where only remission is at stake

confidence.notes: Permission-only decision; substantive appeal merits were not finally determined.

notes: Traveller encampment possession and interim homelessness accommodation challenge; both grounds dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Maughan v Leicester: traveller encampment eviction and interim housing
key_facts: Mr Maughan, a traveller with a wife and four children, unlawfully encamped on Leicester City Council land at Aylestone Playing Fields from October 2003.

The council tolerated the encampment for about four months before deciding in January and confirming in April 2004 to seek possession because of cable burning, scrap activity, nuisance, and loss of the car park.
The claimant made a homelessness application and was offered conventional hostel interim accommodation, which he rejected on cultural grounds.
He challenged both the eviction decisions and the February 2004 interim accommodation offer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of local authority decisions to evict an unauthorised encampment and to offer interim conventional accommodation.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; interim injunction discharged; claimant ordered to pay costs subject to public funding proviso.
enrichment.ratio: A council applying its own enforcement policy may proceed to evict travellers without obtaining every requested health or education report if it had sufficient information for a balanced decision and the additional material would not have changed the outcome; an interim offer of conventional hostel accommodation pending a homelessness decision was lawful where recent history showed no sufficient cultural aversion to bricks and mortar housing.
legal_issues: Whether the council failed to make adequate enquiries before deciding to evict
Whether the April 2004 confirmatory decision mischaracterised medical conditions as stabilised
Whether education disruption and homelessness duties were relevant to the eviction decision
Whether the interim offer of conventional accommodation was unlawful under R (Price) v Carmarthenshire
linked_authorities: R (Price) v Carmarthenshire County Council [2003] EWHC 42 (Admin)
R v Hillingdon London Borough Council ex p McDonagh (1998) 31 HLR 531
R v London Borough of Barnet ex p Grumbridge (1992) 24 HLR 433
R v Lewisham London Borough Council ex p Akinsola (1999) 32 HLR 414

confidence.notes: Both main issues and dismissal are clearly reasoned. Final intentional homelessness decision was under separate review.

notes: Open-court care proceedings after criminal acquittal; shaken baby causation and standard of proof analysis is detailed but fact-intensive.

enrichment.short_title: Local Authority v S: shaken baby causation after criminal acquittal
key_facts: A 20-month-old child X died from head injuries while in the care of W, the partner of X's mother; W was acquitted of murder and manslaughter in 2003.
The local authority sought a care order for surviving child T, requiring findings on how X died.
Medical experts agreed the injuries were acceleration/deceleration with rotational forces, likely non-accidental absent a reliable explanation.
W's account was unreliable; the judge found he culpably pushed X away with force causing fatal injury but without malevolent intent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Public family law fact-finding hearing in care proceedings following criminal acquittal, heard in open court with reporting restrictions.
enrichment.outcome: Threshold criteria satisfied: non-accidental head injury found on balance of probabilities; mother exonerated; welfare stage to follow.
enrichment.ratio: Family courts apply the balance of probabilities, not the criminal standard; an acquittal does not preclude different civil findings; where medical experts agree non-accidental injury is overwhelmingly probable absent a reliable explanation, and the carer's account is unreliable, a finding of culpable but non-intentional infliction may be made despite jury acquittal on manslaughter.
legal_issues: Whether family proceedings may reach different conclusions from a criminal acquittal
The standard and burden of proof in care proceedings
Causation of subdural haematomas, retinal haemorrhages, and other injuries
Whether W's explanation could account for the head injury
Whether the mother posed any risk to T

notes: Planning enforcement appeal on second-bite, rolling immunity, and notice correction; permission granted and appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Sanders v SoS: planning enforcement notice and ten-year immunity
key_facts: Epping Forest District Council issued a second enforcement notice in 2003 alleging mixed commercial use of Galley Hill Yard without planning permission.
An earlier 1999 notice had been quashed because the council changed its case at inquiry.
The inspector treated the second notice as issued afresh rather than under section 171B(4) second-bite provisions and corrected its wording under section 176.
The inspector found no ten-year rolling immunity because activities fell to a low ebb between 1993 and 1996 and relevant uses had not commenced by mid-1983.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 289 appeal with permission granted after rolled-up hearing against an inspector's decision upholding an enforcement notice.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; substantive appeal dismissed; appellant ordered to pay the Secretary of State's costs; council's costs refused.
enrichment.ratio: An enforcement notice goes outside second-bite protection where it alleges a materially wider mix of uses than an earlier notice rather than merely correcting a misdescription; immunity under section 171B(3) requires continuous use throughout the ten-year period preceding the notice, and a period during which enforcement would have been unreasonable breaks continuity.
legal_issues: Whether the second notice was a valid second-bite notice under section 171B(4)(b)
Whether the inspector lawfully corrected the notice under section 176 without injustice
Whether ten-year rolling immunity had accrued
Whether the inspector's findings on use commencement in the early 1980s were perverse
Whether requiring removal of fences was lawful

notes: Admiralty jurisdiction set aside; arbitrator appointed under section 18 despite parallel Spanish criminal investigation.

enrichment.short_title: Atlanska Plovidba v Consignaciones: deck cargo arbitration appointment
key_facts: A Gottwald crane shipped on deck from Gijon to Aviles on the Lapad toppled during discharge, killing the crane driver and damaging vessels.
Spanish criminal investigation proceedings commenced; claimants also issued Admiralty proceedings seeking declarations of non-liability.
The contract was governed by a Conelinebooking note with London arbitration clause 17, not the bill of lading jurisdiction clause.
The defendant challenged English court jurisdiction; claimants sought appointment of a sole arbitrator under section 18.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Concurrent applications to set aside service in Admiralty proceedings and to appoint an arbitrator under section 18 of the Arbitration Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Service set aside for lack of jurisdiction; sole arbitrator appointed in London.
enrichment.ratio: Where parties' rights are governed by a booking note containing a London arbitration agreement, there is no English court jurisdiction over a Spanish-domiciled defendant; the court should normally exercise its section 18 discretion to appoint an arbitrator unless arbitration cannot fairly resolve the dispute, and pending foreign criminal proceedings do not justify refusing appointment.
legal_issues: Whether the booking note or bill of lading governed the parties' relationship
Whether claimants gave effective notice of arbitration under section 16
Whether the court had jurisdiction to appoint an arbitrator under section 18
Whether parallel Spanish criminal proceedings justified refusing appointment
Whether a notice referring to the wrong contract document was ineffective

notes: Second permission to appeal alleging will witnessing fraud; Taylor v Lawrence and costs injustice issues are complex and interlocutory.

enrichment.short_title: Couwenbergh v Valkova: second permission to appeal on will fraud
key_facts: Mrs Alice Adam's October 1990 will leaving her estate to Dr Bilyana Valkova was pronounced valid by Carnwath J in 1998 after a challenge by Petrus Couwenbergh.
Couwenbergh was ordered to pay about £107,000 costs to the Legal Services Commission; Dutch freezing orders were obtained.
Police investigation produced statements from witnesses Lorenzo and Orazio Di Gregorio denying they witnessed the testatrix sign the will and alleging forged confirmation letters.
Couwenbergh made a second application for permission to appeal under Taylor v Lawrence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second application for permission to appeal alleging fraudulent attestation and seeking to reopen probate and costs orders.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; costs of the application costs in the appeal; mediation urged.
enrichment.ratio: Where there is a real prospect that fresh evidence of forged will attestation and perversion of justice would be admitted under Ladd v Marshall, and that a substantial injustice may have occurred especially in relation to costs, a second permission application may succeed under Taylor v Lawrence even though a fresh action is the usual remedy for fraud.
legal_issues: Whether Taylor v Lawrence criteria for reopening a final judgment are met
Whether Di Gregorio brothers' fresh evidence should be admitted
Whether the October 1990 will was invalid for want of due execution
Whether the earlier Doyle-attested will would succeed if the Italian-attested will failed
Whether a fresh action or appeal retrial is the effective remedy for alleged fraud

notes: Rolling exclusive supply agreement construction and mandatory injunction appeal; declaration varied on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: G&A v HN Jewelry: construction of three-year rolling supply contract
key_facts: G&A and HN Jewellery (Asia) Ltd entered a May 2001 exclusive supply agreement for UK, Irish, and Gibraltar jewellery distribution, expressed as 'for three years rolling, commencing on 1 January 2001'.
HN gave notice in August 2003 terminating at 31 December 2003; G&A contended three years' notice was required.
Before trial HN restructured the group, transferring assets and incorporating HNJ (Europe) Ltd, leading to joinder of further defendants.
Crane J declared the contract terminable only on three years' notice and granted mandatory injunctions preserving exclusivity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal treated as full appeal on contract construction and interim mandatory injunctions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on construction: contract terminable by notice at end of the first year of any three-year period, leaving two years to run; suggested notice period about six weeks from 15 November; permission to appeal against mandatory injunctions refused.
enrichment.ratio: A 'three years rolling' exclusive supply agreement is best construed as renewing in three-year blocks unless reasonable notice is given at the end of a year to terminate at the following 31 December with two years remaining; neither a day-by-day three-year lock-in nor termination on short notice at any time fits the annual planning structure of the contract.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'three years rolling' in the exclusive supply agreement
Whether termination required three years' notice from any date
Whether reasonable notice could terminate at any time after the initial three-year period
Whether mandatory interlocutory injunctions were too uncertain in form
linked_authorities: Redland Bricks Ltd v Morris [1970] AC 652
Zockoll Group Ltd v Mercury Communications Ltd [1998] Fleet Street Reports 354
Nottingham Building Society v Eurodynamics Systems [1993] F.S.R. 468
